name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 15

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: Old friend guarding equipment at home, in the first place

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so the next pieces sit inside the old friend

blocks.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
a rig is a set of equipment
at home means in
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: A former companion first kept the kit safe at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally means at first or initially, the same sense as in the first place.

clue.text: Fascinates one doctor in case of rabies

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the next word are kept
in places these pieces inside the outer shell

blocks.note: the first and last letters of rabies
the Roman numeral for one
a vet is an animal doctor

explanation.surface: A medic finds a rabies case absorbing.
explanation.walkthrough: A vet is the apt doctor for rabies, which helps the surface hang together.
explanation.definitionFit: To rivet someone is to hold their attention completely, which is to fascinate them.

clue.text: Pushing, being in debt to support English pound

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
someone owing money is in debt

explanation.surface: Pressuring someone while in hock to prop up sterling.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, to support means to sit underneath, so the debt piece comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Elbowing is pushing one's way forward with the elbows, a form of shoving.

clue.text: Protection for lap top?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cover or case for a laptop computer
setter's reading: a cloth spread over the top of the lap while eating

explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'lap top', the computer becomes the top of someone's lap, kept clean during a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin is laid over the thighs at table to protect clothing from spills.

clue.text: The way to absorb firm at nil cost, and with no penalty

indicators.note: to absorb is to soak something up inside, so the firm goes inside the way

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
something free costs nothing

explanation.surface: A merger at no charge, with no penalty clause attached.
explanation.definitionFit: To get off scot-free is an idiom for escaping punishment entirely.

clue.text: How to make a living from pot, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is spoken or heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: an urn is a pot, and in British speech it sounds like the solution

explanation.surface: Advice on making money from pottery, or from cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' hints at selling drugs, but it is a vessel, an urn.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to receive pay for work, which is how one makes a living.

clue.text: Showing favouritism, section one has a likely leader

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word before it is wanted

blocks.note: a part is a section of something
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
the first letter of likely

explanation.surface: A biased remark that one department already has a probable boss lined up.
explanation.definitionFit: Being partial means being biased towards one side, which is what favouritism is.

clue.text: First class coach supporting election in America?

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting piece holds the other up from below, so it is written second

blocks.note: a primary is a US election to choose a party's candidate
to school someone is to coach or train them

explanation.surface: A luxury bus laid on to back an American election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, supporting puts the coach underneath, after the election. 'First class coach' reads as a luxury carriage, but the definition is just 'First class'.
explanation.definitionFit: A primary school is where children take their first classes, so it is literally a place of first class.

clue.text: Rickety chair included in bill is very old

indicators.note: a rickety thing is shaky and falling apart, so its letters fall into a new order
something included in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
the five letters of chair, rearranged

explanation.surface: An invoice listing a wobbly chair is a sign of very old furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic describes something belonging to a much earlier, antiquated period.

clue.text: Examples of hybrid departments

blocks.note: a cross is a hybrid of two breeds
sections are departments of an organisation

explanation.surface: A list illustrating mixed-discipline university departments.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-section is a representative sample, so cross-sections are examples drawn from a whole.

clue.text: Foreign Legion on track at last, getting the hot seat

indicators.note: foreign suggests something strange and unfamiliar, so these letters are made strange by reordering
at last points to the final letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the final letter of track

explanation.surface: A legionnaire on the race track finally lands in a position of tough scrutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The hot seat' sounds like the idiom for a pressured position, but it is meant literally: an INGLENOOK is a seat built into the corner beside an open fire.
explanation.definitionFit: An inglenook is a recess beside a fireplace where people sit to keep warm, literally a hot seat.

clue.text: Dance beat with verve

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go means energy or verve

explanation.surface: An instruction to dance to the rhythm with energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a musical pulse here, but it means thrash, as in tanning someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is a ballroom dance that originated in Argentina.

clue.text: Workers accept posh relations

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: worker ants are the crossword's stock workers
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: Employees grudgingly take on their boss's upper-class relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the old 'U and non-U' distinction in British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunts are female relatives, so they are among one's relations.

clue.text: Sign — or amuseum will accept a person knowing nothing!

indicators.note: the words will accept, or take in, the solution, which lies inside them across the word breaks

blocks.note: the letters run from inside sign through or into the start of museum

explanation.surface: A notice saying a museum will even let in someone utterly uninformed.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue runs 'a museum' together; the letters span 'sIGN OR A MUSeum'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant person, someone who knows very little.

clue.text: Removed ina spell of bowling?

indicators.note: removed can be read as re-moved, moved again, so the letters are shifted round

blocks.note: all ten letters, the signal word included, taken as written

explanation.surface: A batsman dismissed during a bowler's stint.
explanation.walkthrough: The signal word is part of its own fodder, which the question mark owns up to. An over is a set of six balls in cricket; a maiden is one with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden over is a cricket over of six balls from which the batting side scores no runs.

clue.text: The former students get home and George starts screaming

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that opening letter is taken

blocks.note: ye is the archaic form of the
L for learner, doubled for the plural
to be in is to be at home
the first letter of George

explanation.surface: Alumni arrive home and George begins shrieking at them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The former' looks like it refers back to someone, but it means the old form of 'the'. L is the learner plate on a British learner driver's car.
explanation.definitionFit: Yelling is shouting loudly, close in sense to screaming.

clue.text: Hotel, you say, close to job centre by implication

indicators.note: you say means as it sounds when spoken, so a letter standing for the word you is used
the centre of a word is its middle letter, so only that one is taken

blocks.note: an inn is a small hotel
the letter U sounds like you
the close of something is its end
the middle letter of job

explanation.surface: Someone claims a hotel is handy for the jobcentre, though only hinting at it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job centre' reads as the British unemployment office, but it is just the middle of the word job.
explanation.definitionFit: An innuendo is a hint or insinuation, a remark made by implication rather than directly.

clue.text: Leader lost in escape before team find area that's sheltered

indicators.note: losing its leader means the word drops its opening letter

blocks.note: to flee is to escape
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A captain gone missing during a breakout, the rest of the squad look for cover.
explanation.definitionFit: The lee side is the side away from the wind, so it is the sheltered area.

clue.text: Period clock under sentence?

indicators.note: in a down clue whatever sits under another word comes after it in the entry

blocks.note: a life sentence is a prison term, so life is a sentence
to clock is to time something

explanation.surface: A prisoner watching the clock throughout his term.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, under puts the clock below the sentence, after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifetime is the period of time someone lives.

clue.text: Withdrawing, seeing 15 not working

blocks.note: the answer to 15 across means shouting, and so does crying
a machine that is off is not working

explanation.surface: Someone backs out after seeing a colleague's tantrum stop them functioning.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 15 across, YELLING, whose synonym crying is the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry off is an idiom for backing out of a commitment, so crying off is withdrawing.

clue.text: Advance that's partially drawn of course in reverse

indicators.note: partially means only part of the words is used, a run of letters lying within them
in reverse means read backwards, from right to left

blocks.note: the run of letters from drawn through the start of of

explanation.surface: A drawing partly done, naturally running the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: Onward means moving forward, which is to advance.

clue.text: Noisily speculated about visitor

indicators.note: noisily means heard out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: speculated means guessed, which sounds just like the solution

explanation.surface: Loud gossip about who the visitor might be.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest is someone who visits by invitation, a visitor.

clue.text: Guy was gutted — the speed of turn around!

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters of the word

blocks.note: the first and last letters of guy
rate means speed

explanation.surface: A man devastated by how fast things span round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, but here it means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to revolve or spin, turning round and round.

clue.text: Inthe past, accepted fashionable weight

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so the second piece goes inside the first

blocks.note: once means at some time in the past
U means upper-class, and so smart or fashionable

explanation.surface: Once upon a time, being a stylish weight was socially acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is a unit of weight in the imperial system, a sixteenth of a pound.

clue.text: Negative response to a French word

blocks.note: no is a negative response
un is French for a

explanation.surface: Turning down a French term.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun is a naming word, one of the parts of speech.

clue.text: Game of pool

blocks.note: surface reading: a round of the table game with cue and balls
setter's reading: a team sport played in a swimming pool

explanation.walkthrough: Pool here is not the billiards-style table game but a swimming pool, and the game is the one played there.
explanation.definitionFit: Water polo is a ball game for two teams of swimmers, played in a swimming pool.

clue.text: West coast city less than clean!

blocks.note: Los Angeles, on the US west coast
under means below or less than

explanation.surface: A grumble that a Californian city is not quite spotless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less than clean' reads as one phrase meaning dirty, but the definition is clean alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To launder is to wash and iron clothes, that is, to clean them.

clue.text: "Trust me!" comic says none too clearly

indicators.note: comic means comical or absurd, so the letters before it are played around with

blocks.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A comedian mumbles an unconvincing 'Trust me!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' looks like the speaker, a comedian, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To mutter is to speak quietly and indistinctly, not clearly.
